title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 43
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: What the Wheel Runs On
passages.text:
A. A road is a drainage structure that happens to carry traffic, and almost every failure of one is a failure to keep water out. Water beneath a surface softens the material supporting it, and a load passing overhead then pumps that softened material outwards until the surface loses support and breaks. The engineers who first understood this achieved more by building slightly raised, well-drained roads of graded stone than any amount of paving had achieved before.

B. Size grading mattered as much as drainage and is less obvious. A layer of stones of similar large size shifts under load because the pieces can move past one another; a mixture in which smaller fragments fill the spaces between larger ones locks together and behaves almost as a solid. The insight that a road's strength lies in how its material is sorted rather than in how heavy the individual pieces are was not intuitive and had to be demonstrated.

C. Binding the surface was originally a response to dust rather than to traffic. A well-made stone road produced clouds of it, ruining crops beside the road and choking anyone using it, and the first tars and oils were applied to hold the dust down. That they also sealed the surface against water and held the stones together was discovered afterwards, and the modern sealed road descends from a nuisance remedy.

D. Damage does not rise in proportion to weight, and this single fact governs how roads are paid for. The wear a vehicle causes rises very steeply with its axle load, so a heavy lorry does damage thousands of times greater than a car, and cars in any number do almost nothing to a road built for freight. Almost all road wear is caused by a small fraction of vehicles, which is why charging by weight and axle configuration is the only cost-reflective way to fund maintenance.

E. Maintenance economics have a shape that guarantees deferral. Repairing a surface before it fails costs a fraction of rebuilding it afterwards, and the failure is invisible for years while the deterioration proceeds beneath. Budgets under pressure postpone the cheap intervention because nothing appears to happen, and the resulting bill arrives later, larger, and against a different administration.

F. The surface is now being asked to do things it was never designed for. Quieter surfaces reduce noise for those living alongside and wear out faster; porous surfaces manage runoff and clog; lighter-coloured surfaces reduce heat in cities and cost more. Each is a real improvement in one dimension purchased with a loss in another, and the choice between them is a local judgement rather than a technical answer.

passages.title: The Ground That Was Always Frozen
passages.text:
Permafrost is defined by time rather than by temperature at any moment: it is ground that has remained below freezing for at least two consecutive years, and much of it has been frozen for far longer than that. It underlies a substantial fraction of the northern land surface, it is not the same as ice, and it is not uniformly frozen throughout — a layer near the surface thaws each summer and refreezes each winter, and the depth of that active layer is the quantity that matters most for anything built on it.

The engineering problem is that frozen ground is strong and thawing ground is not. Structures built on permafrost are supported by the ice binding the soil particles, and when that ice melts the ground loses both strength and volume, subsiding unevenly beneath whatever stands on it. The traditional solution is to keep the ground frozen — building on piles driven deep, raising structures so air circulates beneath, and avoiding the heat leakage that a conventional foundation delivers straight into the soil.

Thawing releases carbon that has been out of circulation for a very long time. Plant material that froze before it could decay has accumulated over millennia, and when it thaws, microbes resume the decomposition that was interrupted, producing carbon dioxide where oxygen is available and methane where it is not. The quantity of carbon held this way is large in comparison with annual human emissions, which is why the process attracts attention out of proportion to its visibility.

The rate is where confident statements should stop. Thaw is not uniform: it proceeds gradually over wide areas and abruptly in places where ground ice is concentrated and the surface collapses, and abrupt thaw affects a small share of the area while releasing a disproportionate share of the carbon. Models handle the gradual process reasonably and the abrupt one poorly, and the honest description of the projections is that they carry a wide range with a floor rather than a well-constrained central estimate.

Feedback is the reason the subject matters beyond the region. Carbon released by thawing contributes to warming that causes further thawing, and this loop operates regardless of what emissions do elsewhere once it is under way — which distinguishes it from processes that stop when the cause stops. It is not a sudden event and not reversible on any timescale that concerns policy.

For the people who live there the changes are immediate rather than projected. Buildings crack, roads buckle, pipelines and airstrips require constant repair, coastlines retreat as frozen cliffs collapse, and settlements have been relocated at very great cost. The adaptation problem is arriving decades before the global consequences are settled, and it is being met with resources scaled to a much smaller problem.

passages.title: The Cost of Standing Still
passages.text:
Almost every car spends the overwhelming majority of its existence stationary, and the space it occupies while doing so is provided at a price that bears no relation to its cost. Requirements that new buildings supply a fixed number of parking spaces, and streets where storage is free or nearly so, together constitute one of the largest subsidies in urban policy, and one almost never described as a subsidy by anyone who supports it.

Minimum parking requirements were set by a method that would not survive examination in any other field. Standards were derived from counts of demand at existing sites where parking was already free, which measures how much people use of something that costs nothing rather than how much they need; the resulting numbers were copied between jurisdictions for decades with very little checking. Requirements that oblige a small business to provide more parking area than floor area are common results.

The costs land on people who do not drive. A required space adds substantially to the cost of building a dwelling and that cost enters the rent whether or not the tenant owns a car; land given to storage is not available for housing or anything else; and the resulting lower density makes walking and public transport less viable, which produces the car dependence the requirements were written to accommodate. The policy manufactures the demand it exists to serve.

Free street parking has a distinctive failure that pricing fixes directly. When the price is below the level that clears the space, the shortfall appears as searching: drivers circle looking for a space, and studies of congested districts have attributed a substantial share of traffic in them to this cruising. Setting a price that keeps roughly one space per block open removes the search, and the traffic reduction follows without any change to the number of spaces.

The politics of that reform are unusually well understood. Charging for something that was free is intensely unpopular, and the schemes that have succeeded returned the revenue visibly to the district it came from — repaving, cleaning, lighting, street trees — so that local businesses and residents could see what the money bought. Where revenue disappeared into a general fund, the reform was reversed.

Cities that removed their minimum requirements have not been left without parking, which was the substance of the objection. Developers continued to build spaces where buyers wanted them and stopped where they did not, and the quantity provided fell substantially in dense districts and barely at all elsewhere. Removing a requirement is not a prohibition, and the outcome looks like what people are willing to pay for, which is the ordinary way most things are supplied.
